description: Synthetic development cases testing when bounded native repeat records fit, when ordinary question patterns fit better, when clarification is needed, and when a use is out of scope.

cases.brief: A plant wants to learn where routine maintenance handoffs recently lost time. A technician may recall a few distinct episodes from the last two weeks. The same short fields fit each episode: process stage, coordination barrier, approximate delay band, and possible improvement. The host wants process changes, not a safety log or evaluation of individual workers.

A person preparing for a coaching conversation may want to note several self-chosen goals. Each goal uses the same optional fields: what matters about it, one available support, and a next step or decision to defer. No other person's preferences are being collected.

A worker wants to describe one unusual, non-urgent process problem from last month. The details may not fit a predictable set of fields, and the host needs the worker's own account rather than comparable event records.
A service team needs separate judgments about access, clarity, timeliness, and follow-up. People may rate each differently or skip items that do not apply; there is no forced priority decision.
A manager says, 'Ask staff about all their work problems.' No reference period, repeated unit, decision, or common fields are defined.

A utility wants to collect a separate record for every service interruption a customer experienced during the past year. Some people may have dozens. It has not said whether a sample of events is acceptable or how respondents should choose one.
Operations wants every worker to add a row whenever a maintenance item changes state during a shift, and expects the form to alert the incoming crew when an item is still open.
A site wants repeatable entries for active hazards, exact equipment identifiers, isolation status, and immediate containment so the host can decide whether crews may restart work.

A procurement team wants to understand a supplier's recent delivery delays over one quarter. Respondents may have a few similar examples, and the same non-identifying fields apply to each: broad delivery stage, delay band, operational effect, and improvement idea. The goal is process improvement, not supplier scoring or contract decisions.
A person asks for a repeatable list to record what each household member wants from a shared decision, including reasons they have not directly shared with the respondent.

A clinic wants a patient to add a record for every recent care encounter, including names, diagnoses, and staff-specific judgments. The intended decision, data access, privacy basis, and whether the clinic is asking for service feedback or a clinical diary are unclear.
A community group wants people to consider five possible improvements. People may see several as equally important; the goal is to understand support for each, not force a complete ordered list.
